source.title: Risk of Infection Associated With Administration of Intravenous Iron: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
source.source_type: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials with descriptive nonrandomized-study synthesis
source.source_version_note: Current main PDF includes corrections through January 27, 2025; supplement is the 2021 supplementary file and contains values that differ from the corrected main article.

extraction_metadata.scope_note: Atoms represent review-level methods, pooled meta-analytic findings, author conclusions, limitations, disclosures, and selected material supplement findings. Bibliographic entries and individual underlying-trial results were not atomized as if generated by this review.

atoms.canonical_statement: The review evaluated whether intravenous iron is associated with infection compared with oral iron or no iron.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: OBJECTIVE To examine the risk of infection associated with intravenous iron compared with oral iron or no iron.

atoms.canonical_statement: Randomized clinical trials comparing intravenous iron with oral iron, no iron, or placebo were eligible across patient populations; healthy volunteers were excluded.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: We included randomized clinical trials (RCTs) that compared intravenous iron with oral iron or no iron or placebo.

population.label: Eligible RCT populations
inclusion_criteria: RCT comparing intravenous iron with oral iron, no iron, or placebo

atoms.canonical_statement: Nonrandomized studies were sought when they reported infection, had at least two comparable groups or were quasi-randomized, and were published from 2007 onward.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Therefore, we also searched for nonrandomized studies (NRSs) that met the following criteria: (1) report data on infection, (2) presence of at least 2 comparable groups, (3) quasi-RCTs, and (4) published since January 1, 2007.

population.label: Eligible nonrandomized-study populations
inclusion_criteria: at least 2 comparable groups or quasi-RCT

atoms.canonical_statement: The primary outcome was the proportion of patients who developed an infection.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The primary end point was the proportion of patients who developed an infection.

outcome.definition: proportion of patients who developed an infection

atoms.canonical_statement: Secondary outcomes were hemoglobin, red blood cell transfusion requirements, hospital length of stay, and short-term and long-term mortality.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Secondary outcomes were differences in hemoglobin, RBC transfusion requirements, hospital length of stay, and short-term (≤30 days) and long-term (>30 days) mortality.

outcome.definition: hemoglobin, RBC transfusion requirements, hospital length of stay, short-term and long-term mortality

atoms.canonical_statement: The search covered CENTRAL, Medline, Embase, CINAHL, PubMed ahead-of-print records, Web of Science, and the Transfusion Evidence Library, with ongoing trials sought from ClinicalTrials.gov, CENTRAL, and WHO ICTRP.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: An information specialist (C.D.) searched the following databases: Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) in The Cochrane Library, Medline, Embase, Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL), PubMed (e-publications ahead of print only), Web of Science (1990 onward), and the Transfusion Evidence Library (1950 onward).

atoms.canonical_statement: Two reviewers independently screened titles, abstracts, and full texts, resolving disagreements through discussion.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The same 2 reviewers then independently screened the full text reports for inclusion. Disagreements were resolved through discussion.

atoms.canonical_statement: Pairs of reviewers independently extracted data and assessed risk of bias; disagreements were resolved by discussion or a third reviewer.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Data were extracted onto standardized and prepiloted forms for RCTs and NRSs by pairs of 2 reviewers

atoms.canonical_statement: RCT risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool and nonrandomized studies with ROBINS-I.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Risk of bias for RCTs was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool.

atoms.canonical_statement: Eligible RCTs were pooled with a random-effects model; infection, mortality, and transfusion requirement were reported as risk ratios and continuous outcomes as mean differences.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Data from RCTs that fulfilled the eligibility criteria were pooled for meta-analysis with a random-effects model.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors prespecified subgroup analyses by clinical setting, baseline iron profile, dose schedule, preparation, and cumulative dose, and a sensitivity analysis restricted to trials at low overall risk of bias.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: We performed a sensitivity analysis for infection by only including trials judged to be at overall low risk of bias.

atoms.canonical_statement: GRADE was used to assess certainty of evidence for the primary infection outcome.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The GRADE (Grades of Recommendation, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach was used to assess the overall quality of evidence for the primary outcome of infection.

atoms.canonical_statement: The systematic review included 162 studies with 39,908 participants: 154 RCTs with 32,762 participants and 8 nonrandomized studies with 7,146 participants.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A total of 162 studies with 39 908 participants were included in this systematic review, of which 154 were RCTs (32 762 participants) and 8 were NRSs (7146 participants).

atoms.canonical_statement: The median RCT size was 111 participants, and the largest clinical settings were obstetrics, surgery, and chronic kidney disease.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The median number of participants in the included RCTs was 111 (IQR, 14-2534).

atoms.canonical_statement: The included RCTs spanned multiple continents and clinical settings; iron sucrose and ferric carboxymaltose were the most common preparations.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The most common iron preparations evaluated were iron sucrose (n = 68) and ferric carboxymaltose (n = 51).

atoms.canonical_statement: Risk-of-bias concerns were common, particularly for blinding and allocation concealment.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The high risk of bias was most frequently attributable to insufficient blinding of participants, study personnel, or outcome assessors or not providing sufficient information for a decision.

atoms.canonical_statement: Across 64 RCTs and 19,322 participants, intravenous iron increased infection risk versus oral iron or no iron, with RR 1.16 (95% CI 1.03 to 1.29; I² 36%; P=.003).

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Intravenous iron was associated with an increased risk of infection when compared with oral iron or no iron (RR, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.03-1.29; I2 = 36%; P = .003)

population.label: RCT participants contributing to infection meta-analysis

atoms.canonical_statement: The corrected main article reports an absolute infection excess of 16 per 1,000 people with intravenous iron, with 95% CI 3 to 29 more per 1,000.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: In absolute terms, 16 more people per 1000 population (95% CI, 3-29) will experience an infection when intravenous iron is used

population.label: RCT participants contributing to infection meta-analysis

atoms.canonical_statement: In the prespecified low-risk-of-bias sensitivity analysis, the infection estimate was RR 1.13 (95% CI 0.97 to 1.32; I² 36%; P=.08) across 16 RCTs and 8,561 participants.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: the RR was 1.13 (95% CI, 0.97-1.32; I2 = 36%; P = .08; 16 RCTs; 8561 participants)

atoms.canonical_statement: In the inflammatory bowel disease subgroup, intravenous iron was associated with higher infection risk, RR 1.73 (95% CI 1.11 to 2.71; I² 0%; P=.02) across 6 RCTs and 908 participants.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Subgroup analysis by clinical setting found evidence of an increased risk of infection in patients with IBD (RR, 1.73; 95% CI, 1.11-2.71; I2 = 0%; P = .02; 6 RCTs; 908 participants)

atoms.canonical_statement: The review found no evidence that baseline ferritin, hemoglobin, transferrin saturation, study year, or iron preparation materially modified infection risk.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Metaregression found no evidence of an interaction between baseline ferritin level, hemoglobin level, transferrin saturation, study year, and risk of infection

atoms.canonical_statement: For trials comparing intravenous iron with oral iron, the infection forest plot pooled to RR 1.26 (95% CI 1.09 to 1.44).

population.label: RCT participants in IV iron versus oral iron infection forest plot

atoms.canonical_statement: For trials comparing intravenous iron with no iron, the infection forest plot pooled to RR 1.08 (95% CI 0.92 to 1.26).

population.label: RCT participants in IV iron versus no iron infection forest plot

atoms.canonical_statement: Infection definitions and reporting were inconsistent: 49 RCTs did not provide an a priori definition, 7 used pragmatic investigator-defined criteria, and no RCT reported positive microbiology culture data.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Forty-nine RCTs did not provide a definition a priori.

atoms.canonical_statement: Intravenous iron increased hemoglobin at study endpoint by a mean 0.57 g/dL versus oral iron or no iron (95% CI 0.50 to 0.64; I² 94%; P<.001).

population.label: Participants in pooled hemoglobin analysis shown in Table 2

atoms.canonical_statement: Intravenous iron increased the probability of treatment response, as defined by study authors, with RR 1.46 (95% CI 1.32 to 1.60; I² 92%; P<.001).
Intravenous iron reduced the risk of requiring red blood cell transfusion, RR 0.83 (95% CI 0.76 to 0.89; I² 15%; P<.001).

population.label: Participants in RBC transfusion requirement analysis shown in Table 2

atoms.canonical_statement: Intravenous iron reduced the mean number of red blood cells transfused versus no iron by 0.20 units, MD -0.20 (95% CI -0.32 to -0.08; I² 81%; P<.001).

population.label: Participants in mean RBC transfused analysis

atoms.canonical_statement: Short-term mortality did not differ significantly with intravenous iron, RR 0.99 (95% CI 0.69 to 1.42; I² 0%; P=.73).

population.label: Participants represented by Table 2 short-term mortality arms

atoms.canonical_statement: Long-term mortality did not differ significantly with intravenous iron, RR 0.94 (95% CI 0.75 to 1.18; I² 0%; P=.63).
Hospital length of stay did not differ significantly with intravenous iron, MD -0.43 days (95% CI -1.10 to 0.24; I² 50%; P=.05).

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: MD, −0.43 days; 95% CI, −1.10 to 0.24 days; I2 = 50%; P = .05; 8 RCTs; 1690 participants

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors concluded that intravenous iron was associated with increased infection risk and that this risk should be weighed against anemia treatment and transfusion-reduction benefits.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: intravenous iron administration was associated with an increased risk of infection, which must be considered alongside the potential benefit of treating anemia.

atoms.canonical_statement: Clinical and methodological heterogeneity and inconsistent infection reporting may limit understanding of the true nature and extent of infection risk.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: This study also has limitations, which can be attributed to the clinical and methodological differences and variations in infection reporting between the included studies

atoms.canonical_statement: Updating a previous systematic review may increase type I error from repeated significance testing.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Updating the previous systematic review may lead to type 1 error as a result of multiplicity attributable to repeated significance testing.

atoms.canonical_statement: The review did not test whether the observed hemoglobin improvement translated into better health-related quality of life.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: we did not assess whether this improvement translated into improved health-related quality of life

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Funding/Support: Dr Shah is currently supported by National Institute for Health Research Doctoral Research Fellowship NIHR-DRF-2017-10-094.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Conflict of Interest Disclosures: Dr Acheson reported receiving grant support from Syner-Med (UK), Vifor Pharma (Switzerland), and Pharmacosmos A/S (Denmark)

atoms.canonical_statement: The current main PDF records corrections on January 11, 2022 and December 9, 2024, plus a January 27, 2025 notice that reanalysis after retraction of one included study did not change the reported results.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Correction: This meta-analysis was published before 1 of the included studies76 was retracted. A reanalysis without that study does not affect the reported results.

atoms.canonical_statement: Among the 8 nonrandomized studies, infection findings were mixed and risk of bias was generally moderate; confounding was a major concern.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Overall risk of bias was moderate for seven NRS and only one study was deemed to be at overall low risk of bias.

atoms.canonical_statement: The original 2021 supplement GRADE table reports infection RR 1.17 (95% CI 1.04 to 1.31), 19,480 participants, and 17 more infections per 1,000; these values differ from the corrected main article.

atoms.canonical_statement: Supplement eTable 6 found no statistically significant meta-regression association between infection risk and ferritin, transferrin saturation, hemoglobin, or study year.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Meta-regression analyses of ferritin, transferrin saturation, haemoglobin and study year on log risk ratio on infection.
